source.authors: José Augusto Pereira Carneiro Muniz, Luana Modesto de Athaide, Bruno Duarte Gomes, Barbara L. Finlay, Luiz Carlos de Lima Silveira
source.title: Ganglion Cell and Displaced Amacrine Cell Density Distribution in the Retina of the Howler Monkey (Alouatta caraya)

where: Results, Ganglion cell density along the horizontal and vertical meridians of the Alouatta retina
method: Nissl-stained (cresyl violet) flat-mounted retinas; ganglion cells counted by light microscopy along 12 radial directions from the fovea
conditions: Five adult male Alouatta caraya from the breeding colony of the Centro Nacional de Primatas (Ananindeua, Para, Brazil), bred and kept in the colony until the experiment (captive-bred, not wild); ages not reported. Six flat-mounted retinas (left retinas of four animals, both retinas of the fifth); five counted over their whole extent and a sixth only in midperipheral and peripheral regions. The means and standard deviations for the central 3 mm are plotted for N = 5 retinas (preceding Results sentence). Cells counted along 12 radial directions at 30 degree intervals from the fovea with a 100x oil objective, sampling every 0.25 mm for the first 3 mm; counting fields 1,537 square micrometres within 1.5 mm of the fovea, 9,604 from 1.75 to 5 mm and 38,416 from 6 mm to the periphery. Retinas fixed (10% formaldehyde perfusion) then exposed to formaldehyde vapour at 60 C; areal shrinkage in four retinas averaged 4.8 +/- 4.3% (range 1 to 11%) and no correction was applied to densities because, the authors state, shrinkage occurred only along retinal borders and the relieving cuts, so the counted regions are taken as unshrunk. There was no consistent difference in dorsal versus ventral ganglion cell density (no statistical test printed). Values are mean +/- SD: nasal 44,963 +/- 3,089; temporal 42,191 +/- 2,063; dorsal 43,825 +/- 788; ventral 40,673 +/- 2,669. The abstract states the peak as 'reaching 40,700-45,200 cells/mm2' at 0.5 mm 'between the fovea and optic nerve head', slightly different from the Results means (upper figure 45,200 versus 44,963; the Results give four named directions, the abstract does not). No acuity (cycles per degree) estimate is reported in the paper. Density is for ganglion cells; displaced amacrine cells are counted separately (peaks 2,050 to 3,100 cells/mm2 in the abstract).
quote: Ganglion cell density reached maximum values in the foveal slope: 44,963±3,089, 42,191±2,063, 43,825±788, and 40,673±2,669 cells/mm2 at 0.5 mm nasal, temporal, dorsal, and ventral to the fovea, respectively.

source.authors: Susanne Schwarze, Friederike Steenken, Nadine Thiele, Dmitry Kobylkov, Nele Lefeldt, David Dreyer, Nils-Lasse Schneider, Henrik Mouritsen
source.title: Migratory blackcaps can use their magnetic compass at 5 degrees inclination, but are completely random at 0 degrees inclination

method: Emlen funnel orientation tests (modified aluminium funnels, scratch paper) of caged night-migratory birds in grounded aluminium-lined huts acting as Faraday cages under controlled magnetic fields, inclination 67 (local), 5 and 0 degrees, horizontal component pointing to magnetic north (NMF) or rotated -120 degrees (CMF); Rayleigh tests
value: oriented at 5 degrees inclination as well as in the normal 67 degree inclined field (Oldenburg)
quote: At 5° inclination, the birds oriented as well as they did in the normal 67° inclined field in Oldenburg.
conditions: Wild-caught Eurasian blackcaps (August 2013 and 2014, within 1 km of the University of Oldenburg, Germany), housed indoors under local photoperiod; 26 birds in total (summarising page tool). Groups and N per condition as printed: spring 2014 5 deg NMF N = 11, 5 deg CMF N = 11, 0 deg NMF N = 11, 0 deg CMF N = 12; autumn 2014 67 deg NMF N = 11, 5 deg NMF N = 10, 5 deg CMF N = 9 (0 deg omitted in autumn); spring 2015 67 deg NMF and CMF N = 13 each, 0 deg NMF N = 9, 0 deg CMF N = 12. Rayleigh tests, birds tested in a field with fluxgate monitoring (tool summary: control and 0 deg tests semi-randomly intermixed; evaluators blind to the direction in a double-blind replication; about 25% of nights classed inactive and excluded). Sex and age not read. Stimulus is a set (nominal) inclination, with field strength held constant (tool summary), not a separately reported measured value. 5 deg results (Results, Rayleigh): spring 2014 5 deg NMF mean 47 deg, r = 0.61, N = 11, p < 0.05; 5 deg CMF mean 294 deg, r = 0.57, N = 11, p < 0.05 (turned accordingly after the -120 deg rotation; Mardia-Watson-Wheeler 5 deg NMF vs CMF W = 6.402, df = 2, p = 0.041); autumn 2014 67 deg NMF 235 deg, r = 0.55, N = 11, p < 0.05; 5 deg NMF 204 deg, r = 0.57, N = 10, p < 0.05; 5 deg CMF 78 deg, r = 0.73, N = 9, p < 0.01; spring 2015 67 deg NMF 38 deg, r = 0.66, N = 13, p < 0.01; 67 deg CMF 284 deg, r = 0.79, N = 13, p < 0.001 (NMF vs CMF W = 19.965, df = 2, p < 0.001). Autumn 2014 5 deg NMF vs CMF W = 12.348, df = 2, p < 0.002; 67 deg NMF vs 5 deg NMF not different (W = 0.574, df = 2, p > 0.607). The 5 and 67 deg fields were run in the same season only in autumn 2014 (spring 2014 had no 67 deg group, spring 2015 no 5 deg group), and no test of concentration (r) between 5 and 67 deg is printed, so 'as well as' is the authors' reading of similar direction and r. The same birds were tested across conditions (pooled analyses use one mean per bird); scratch papers with observer disagreement were treated as random (about 10%). Contrary result for the same birds: at 0 deg inclination orientation was random in every condition (companion record).

quote: In contrast, they were completely randomly oriented in the horizontal field, showing no sign of bimodality.

source.authors: Julia Bojarinova, Kirill Kavokin, Alexander Pakhomov, Roman Cherbunin, Anna Anashina, Maria Erokhina, Maria Ershova, Nikita Chernetsov
source.title: Magnetic compass of garden warblers is not affected by oscillating magnetic fields applied to their eyes

method: Emlen funnel orientation tests of caged night-migratory birds in a screened non-magnetic chamber, with a portable coil device generating an oscillating magnetic field (OMF, about 5 nT) at the eyes, switched on or off; Rayleigh tests
conditions: First-year garden warblers captured wild during autumn migration on the Courish Spit, Kaliningrad region, Russia; held in individual outdoor cages at least 5 days; birds with nocturnal restlessness selected; tested 23 August to 16 September, 50 min from astronomical twilight (details from a summarising page tool). Phase 1, no device, indoors: mean 216 deg, n = 21, r = 0.38, P = 0.045. In phase 2 the birds passed three types of tests (device on, device off, stationary-coil OMF without device, the coil test before the device was fitted or after it was removed), so the phase-2 groups are largely the same birds. Device-on direction did not differ from the no-device birds (Mardia-Watson-Wheeler W = 0.15, p = 0.93) or the device-off birds (W = 0.49, p = 0.78). Each bird was tested one to four times until it showed directional selectivity. Switched-off device (dummy of equal weight): alpha = 164 deg, n = 11, r = 0.51, P = 0.056, just below the significance level (so the off-device control group itself was not significantly oriented). Switched-on device: n = 14 (the quoted result). Contrary result: the same birds placed in a homogeneous 5 nT OMF from stationary coils (no device, mean 106 deg, n = 12, r = 0.11, P = 0.86) were disoriented. Of 22 birds fitted with devices, 21 were active. Device tests double-blind until all experiments ended; birds with fewer than 40 scratches or judged disoriented were excluded; Rayleigh tests at 5%. The order of test conditions is not described; the OMF strength was nominal 5 nT, checked before and after tests with a ferrite antenna and oscilloscope (summary). The per-bird breakdown across conditions is in the Supplementary Material, not read; testing to a criterion with disoriented birds excluded favours oriented group results.
quote: Extraordinarily, when the device was on, they were not disoriented either: the birds showed migratory orientation appropriate for autumn migratory season (α = 189°, n = 14, r = 0.49, P = 0.03; Fig. 2D).
note: Whole Results sentence of 31 words, read in two abutting pieces in one response and again with the same join on a second response (said in pieces). The abstract sentence 'Surprisingly, the birds were not disoriented and showed the seasonally appropriate migratory direction.' reports the same result. Null-type finding: the authors read it as showing the oscillating-field effect on the eye is absent for the magnetic compass here. Family and order as on main (Sylviidae, Passeriformes); Sylvia borin not listed in gbif-names.tsv, name as used on main. value: control birds kept without natural celestial cues remained unable to orient

source.authors: Bianca Alert, Andreas Michalik, Nadine Thiele, Michael Bottesch, Henrik Mouritsen
source.title: Re-calibration of the magnetic compass in hand-raised European robins (Erithacus rubecula)

method: Emlen funnel orientation tests in aluminium-shielded huts in a simulated geomagnetic field (48,880 nT, 67.5 deg inclination, 0 deg declination); Rayleigh tests; hand-raised birds with or without exposure to natural celestial cues
conditions: 41 nestlings taken from nests near Oldenburg, Lower Saxony, Germany, at 5 to 11 days old (13 in 2010, 13 in 2011, 15 in 2013), hand-raised in a windowless room with a lamp-simulated photoperiod and the geomagnetic field but no natural celestial cues (wild-origin nestlings, hand-raised captive adults). Autumn baseline, all 41 birds in the normal geomagnetic field: not significantly oriented (Rayleigh mean 23 deg, r = 0.17, n = 41, P = 0.295). At the end of February about half were moved to an outdoor aviary with natural celestial cues (experimental, n = 22: 7 in 2011, 6 in 2012, 9 in 2014) and the rest stayed indoors (control, n = 19); the paper does not describe how birds were assigned. Spring tests mid-March to mid-April, one hour, once or twice, up to nine birds per night, both groups mostly tested simultaneously; of 547 spring tests 130 were excluded for low activity, 12 for bimodal and 45 for random orientation; two scorers, a third re-analysed differences over 30 deg (all from a summarising page tool). Control spring result (Results): Rayleigh mean 294 deg, r = 0.08, n = 19, P = 0.895 (disoriented); V test toward the expected 33 deg spring direction V = -0.012, P = 0.529. The control group's orientation was significantly more scattered than the experimental group's (r = 0.08 vs 0.43, P = 0.002; 99% confidence limits 0.11 < r < 0.75 by bootstrapping 19 values from the oriented sample). Experimental birds' mean directions did not differ between the three seasons (Watson-Williams F = 1.307, df = 2, P = 0.294). Contrary comparison: the experimental group oriented in the north-easterly spring direction (mean 56 deg, r = 0.43, n = 22); the Results text prints P = 0.004 but the Fig. 2 caption prints P = 0.017 for the same group, a discrepancy in the paper. Randomisation and handler blinding to group are not described.
quote: In contrast, control birds that were deprived of any natural celestial cues throughout remained unable to orient.
note: Whole abstract sentence of 17 words, returned unbroken on two passes (the sentence before it says birds with celestial-cue access could orient in the spring direction). Null result for the control group. Not on main under this DOI. Family and order (Muscicapidae, Passeriformes) as on main for this species; GBIF ACCEPTED in gbif-names.tsv; main's other Erithacus rubecula sense_magnetic rows have different DOIs (pone.0043271, pone.0020091 pooled with Gallus, and the bpj paper). source.authors: He-Qun Liu, Jing-Kuan Wei, Bo Li, Ming-Shan Wang, Rui-Qi Wu, Joshua D. Rizak, Li Zhong, Lu Wang, Fu-Qiang Xu, Yong-Yi Shen, Xin-Tian Hu, Ya-Ping Zhang
source.title: Divergence of dim-light vision among bats (order: Chiroptera) as estimated by molecular and electrophysiological methods

where: Results, Assessment of absolute visual thresholds
method: flash visual evoked potential (f-VEP) recorded from the visual cortex of restrained, dark-adapted bats; two trains of 180 flashes of 100 ms, ISI 1 to 3 s random, 180 epochs averaged per f-VEP, at 12 intensity levels (−0.95, −1.49, −1.90, −2.45, −2.85, −3.71, −4.77, −6.20, −6.30, −6.37, −6.43 and −6.51 log cd/m2•s) on a gamma-linearised LCD display; threshold defined as the lowest flash intensity that produced an N-P-N structure distinguishable from baseline, so each value is a tested level and the true threshold lies between it and the next lower level
conditions: Bats captured in the wild and housed in large cages, 5 to 6 days acclimation before testing (wild-caught, not lab-bred). This species: insectivorous bat; acute recordings, 4 animals (sex not given), used acutely because they did not survive long after surgery. The next lower tested level was −2.45, so the threshold lies between −1.90 and −2.45 log cd/m2•s. Other species in the same sentence: T. melanopogon -3.71; C. sphinx -6.30; R. leschenaultii -6.37 (log cd/m2 s); the paper's summary paragraph reports the lowest thresholds in Pteropodidae, then Emballonuridae, then insectivorous bats. Dark adaptation 20 min in absolute darkness (<0.25 lx) before recording; deep pentobarbital anaesthesia for electrode implantation, and whether animals were anaesthetised during the recordings is not clear. Luminance values are display-generated stimulus settings; the page text does not say they were measured with a photometer (calculated versus measured not stated), and no photometer is named for the flashes (the only meter named measured room background). Sex stated only for the two chronic species (male); sex of the acute species not reported. n is 2 to 4 per species; whether each species value is per animal, a mean or the lowest across animals is not stated, and no per-animal variation or statistic is given. Recording mode follows the family split: the two pteropodids were recorded chronically and the insectivorous R. affinis and the emballonurid T. melanopogon acutely, because they did not survive long after surgery; the state of anaesthesia during recording is not stated and the authors give no caveat on comparing acute and chronic recordings, so the family ranking is confounded with recording mode.
quote: The absolute visual threshold intensity for each species was −1.90 (log cd/m2•s) for R. affinis, −3.71 (log cd/m2•s) for T. melanopogon and −6.30 and −6.37 (log cd/m2•s) for C. sphinx and R. leschenaultii, respectively.
note: Whole Results sentence of 34 words (count as check.py counts), returned in consecutive pieces in two responses with different split points and the same joined text (said in pieces); the minus signs and the dot in cd/m2 s were checked in the returned text. units: log cd/m2 s (flash visual evoked potential threshold; more negative is more sensitive)

source.authors: He-Qun Liu, Jing-Kuan Wei, Bo Li, Ming-Shan Wang, Rui-Qi Wu, Joshua D. Rizak, Li Zhong, Lu Wang, Fu-Qiang Xu, Yong-Yi Shen, Xin-Tian Hu, Ya-Ping Zhang
source.title: Divergence of dim-light vision among bats (order: Chiroptera) as estimated by molecular and electrophysiological methods

where: Results, Assessment of absolute visual thresholds
method: flash visual evoked potential (f-VEP) recorded from the visual cortex of restrained, dark-adapted bats; two trains of 180 flashes of 100 ms, ISI 1 to 3 s random, 180 epochs averaged per f-VEP, at 12 intensity levels (−0.95, −1.49, −1.90, −2.45, −2.85, −3.71, −4.77, −6.20, −6.30, −6.37, −6.43 and −6.51 log cd/m2•s) on a gamma-linearised LCD display; threshold defined as the lowest flash intensity that produced an N-P-N structure distinguishable from baseline, so each value is a tested level and the true threshold lies between it and the next lower level
conditions: Bats captured in the wild and housed in large cages, 5 to 6 days acclimation before testing (wild-caught, not lab-bred). This species: Pteropodidae; chronic recordings, 2 male animals (C. sphinx 26 and 30 g; R. leschenaultii 75 and 88 g), measured repeatedly. The next lower tested level was −6.43, so the threshold lies between −6.37 and −6.43 log cd/m2•s, and the difference from C. sphinx (−6.30) is one step of the stimulus series on two animals each. Other species in the same sentence: R. affinis -1.90; T. melanopogon -3.71; C. sphinx -6.30 (log cd/m2 s); the paper's summary paragraph reports the lowest thresholds in Pteropodidae, then Emballonuridae, then insectivorous bats. Dark adaptation 20 min in absolute darkness (<0.25 lx) before recording; deep pentobarbital anaesthesia for electrode implantation, and whether animals were anaesthetised during the recordings is not clear. Luminance values are display-generated stimulus settings; the page text does not say they were measured with a photometer (calculated versus measured not stated), and no photometer is named for the flashes (the only meter named measured room background). Sex stated only for the two chronic species (male); sex of the acute species not reported. n is 2 to 4 per species; whether each species value is per animal, a mean or the lowest across animals is not stated, and no per-animal variation or statistic is given. Recording mode follows the family split: the two pteropodids were recorded chronically and the insectivorous R. affinis and the emballonurid T. melanopogon acutely, because they did not survive long after surgery; the state of anaesthesia during recording is not stated and the authors give no caveat on comparing acute and chronic recordings, so the family ranking is confounded with recording mode.
quote: The absolute visual threshold intensity for each species was −1.90 (log cd/m2•s) for R. affinis, −3.71 (log cd/m2•s) for T. melanopogon and −6.30 and −6.37 (log cd/m2•s) for C. sphinx and R. leschenaultii, respectively.
